interment

in-TUR-ment · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Interment is the burial of a corpse in a tomb or grave; the act of interring.

The interment took place at dawn, attended only by close family, per the general's own wishes.

Example

Local zoning rules required a full week's notice before any interment could take place at the historic cemetery, delaying the family's plans.

Interment refers specifically to the act of burying a body -- the formal event of lowering the casket into the ground, not the funeral service itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

burial: Burial is the everyday word for placing a dead body in the ground. Interment means the same act in formal dress -- the word you meet in legal notices, military honors, and obituaries. A family speaks of the burial; the funeral home's paperwork records the interment.

committal: A committal is the brief graveside rite in which a body is formally committed to its resting place -- the final words and prayers said as the casket is lowered. Interment is the physical act itself: actually placing the body in the grave, with or without any words at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

exhumation: the act of digging up a buried body

disinterment: the act of removing a body from its place of burial

Where it sits · how elaborate the laying to rest is

scattering → interment → entombment

scattering vs. interment: Scattering ashes from a hillside takes a single quiet moment and needs no grave at all -- the simplest laying to rest there is, far less elaborate than a formal interment.

entombment vs. interment: Entombment is a step more elaborate than interment: rather than a simple grave in the ground, it means placing a body in a built tomb or vault.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: into (Latin)

Root — ter: earth (from Latin terra, 'earth' -- terra's double r slims to one inside interment)

Suffix — -ment: the act or result of (Latin -mentum)

Put it together: Interment comes from in- ("into") + ter ("earth," from Latin terra) + -ment ("the act of") -- literally "putting into the earth," the formal act of burial.

Use the root in a new word: territory: Wolves are fiercely protective of their territory, chasing off any rival pack that gets too close.
